passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, second week of term.
Shankar joined us on Monday. He uses crutches after a leg surgery and is still getting used to the stairs. On the first two days he ate lunch alone near the classroom door while the others ran to the ground.
On Wednesday, Nikita noticed. She asked me if she could bring a board game to the corridor at lunch. She invited Shankar and three others. They played ludo, and Shankar won twice.
Today Nikita asked if the class could play word games on the ground's steps, so Shankar can join from the bottom step.
I've said yes, and will add it to the timetable.
— Mrs Kulkarni

qa.q: What game did Nikita's group play in the corridor?
qa.a: Ludo.

qa.q: What might Nikita have been feeling when she noticed Shankar eating alone?
qa.a: Nikita probably felt concerned and sorry for Shankar, sitting alone while everyone ran off.

qa.q: What did Nikita do that made room for Shankar?
qa.a: She chose games he could join, brought them to where he could get to, and invited others too.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel when Nikita invites him?
qa.a: Shankar likely feels relieved and welcome, not left out by his crutches.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child making lunch-break games accessible to a new classmate on crutches.

passage:
Dear Diary,
There's a new girl in our class, Trisha. She came from Shillong. She doesn't talk. At lunch she sits at the end of the bench and reads a book with her tiffin still closed.
Today I saw the book. It was about volcanoes. I love volcanoes!
I sat next to her and said, "Is that the one with the Iceland volcano?" She looked up, surprised, and nodded. Then she showed me a picture. Then she opened her tiffin.
Tomorrow I'm going to ask her to sit with our group. Rahil might say she's weird. I'll say she knows more about volcanoes than him.
— Yogesh

qa.q: Where did Trisha come from?
qa.a: Shillong.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling when she looked up, surprised?
qa.a: Trisha felt surprised and a little shy, but pleased that someone shared her interest.

qa.q: What small step helped Yogesh reach Trisha?
qa.a: Starting with the book she was reading gave them something in common to talk about.

qa.q: If you were Trisha, what would you want from the class?
qa.a: Trisha would probably want patience and someone to sit with, without being pushed to talk a lot.

grounding: A child writes about welcoming a shy new classmate through a shared interest.

The kho-kho game at the village school was about to start. Disha, who walks with a limp, sat on the wall as always.
Arohi ran over. "Come play."
"I'm too slow. They'll catch me in a second."
Arohi thought. "Then be the one who sits in the line. You don't have to run far. You just have to watch and jump up when tapped."
Disha hesitated, then took a spot in the sitting line. When Arohi tapped her, she sprang up and caught a boy who thought she wouldn't move.
The whole team cheered. Disha grinned so wide her eyes closed.

qa.q: Where did Disha usually sit during kho-kho?
qa.a: On the wall.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling when she said she was too slow?
qa.a: Disha felt unsure and worried she would be caught quickly and let the team down.

qa.q: What did Arohi do that made room for Disha?
qa.a: She found a role in the game that suited Disha instead of just asking her to run like everyone else.

qa.q: How might the boy who was caught see Disha now?
qa.a: The boy is surprised and may now see Disha as a real player, not someone who just watches.

grounding: A village child finds a way to include a classmate with a limp in kho-kho.

passage:
The cricket match on the colony ground was cut short by rain, and only one end of the pitch was dry. Parul said, "Let Ritu bowl the last over."
"Girls can't bowl properly," muttered Advait, the captain.
Ritu didn't argue. She took the wet ball, dried it on her shirt, and ran in.
The first ball skidded past Advait's bat.
He stared. Then he said, "Okay, that was good."
"Just say 'nice ball'," said Parul. "Not 'for a girl'."
Advait nodded. "Nice ball, Ritu."
Ritu smiled and bowled the next one.

qa.q: What did Ritu dry the wet ball on?
qa.a: Her shirt.

qa.q: What might Advait have been feeling when he stared?
qa.a: Advait was surprised and a bit embarrassed that his remark was wrong.

qa.q: What did Parul suggest, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She told Advait to just say "nice ball" without "for a girl", which treats Ritu with the same respect as any bowler.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel when Advait finally says "Nice ball, Ritu"?
qa.a: Ritu probably feels respected and proud 🏏 that her skill was recognised without mockery.

grounding: On a rain-shortened cricket ground, children move past a gender stereotype about bowling.

passage:
It was cleaning day in the Pune classroom. The teacher gave out jobs.
"Sweeping is girls' work," said Rudra, pushing the broom at Devika.
Devika pushed it back. "Brooms don't know if you're a boy or a girl."
The class laughed. Rudra shrugged and swept.
Later, when Bhavna was stacking chairs, Rudra tugged her plait as a joke. Bhavna turned. "Don't touch my hair. I don't like it."
Rudra's face went red. "Sorry. I thought it was funny."
"Not to me," said Bhavna.
Rudra nodded and went back to sweeping, faster this time.

qa.q: What was Bhavna doing when Rudra tugged her plait?
qa.a: Stacking chairs.

qa.q: What was Rudra feeling when his face went red?
qa.a: Rudra felt embarrassed and ashamed, realising his joke wasn't funny to Bhavna.

qa.q: What did Devika and Bhavna each do well?
qa.a: Devika challenged the idea that sweeping is girls' work, and Bhavna clearly set a boundary about touching her hair.

qa.q: How might Rudra see his classmates after this?
qa.a: Rudra may see that girls expect the same jobs and respect as boys, and that touching without asking isn't okay.

grounding: In an urban classroom, children challenge a gender stereotype and set a physical boundary.

In the market of her small town, Vandana bought a packet of salt from Pema aunty's shop. Pema aunty was busy talking and gave her change for a hundred rupees, but Vandana had given her fifty.
Vandana counted the coins on the way home. Too much. Nobody would ever know. Pema aunty hadn't even looked.
She could buy three ice lollies with it.
She stopped by the tea stall and looked at the coins for a long time. Then she walked back.
"Aunty, you gave me extra." Pema aunty blinked, then laughed. "Arre, I'd have been short tonight! Thank you, beta." She pressed a toffee into her hand.

qa.a: Fifty rupees.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling when she looked at the coins for a long time?
qa.a: Vandana felt tempted and torn between keeping the money and being honest.

qa.q: What would you advise a friend who faces the same choice?

qa.q: How might Pema aunty see Vandana after this?
qa.a: Pema aunty is grateful and will likely trust Vandana more, knowing she is honest even when unwatched.

grounding: A child returns extra change though no one would have known.

passage:
In the quiet street in Haifa, Yosef was kicking his ball against the wall. It bounced wrong and smashed the clay pot on Mr Daniel's step.
Nobody saw. Mr Daniel was at work. Yosef's heart thumped. He could just go inside.
He picked up the pieces and put them in a neat pile. Then he wrote a note: "Mr Daniel, I broke your pot with my ball. I'm sorry. I'll help you plant a new one. — Yosef, number 4."
In the evening, Mr Daniel knocked. Yosef's stomach dropped. But Mr Daniel held up the note. "This took courage." He smiled. "Saturday, then. Bring gloves."

qa.q: What did Yosef's ball smash?
qa.a: The clay pot on Mr Daniel's step.

qa.q: What was Yosef feeling when his stomach dropped?
qa.a: Yosef felt nervous and afraid that Mr Daniel would be angry.

qa.q: What did Yosef's note do that just going inside would not?
qa.a: It admitted the mistake and offered to fix it, which built trust instead of hiding the harm.

qa.q: How does Mr Daniel see Yosef's note?
qa.a: Mr Daniel sees it as brave and honest, which matters more to him than the broken pot.

grounding: A child in Israel admits breaking a neighbour's pot though no one saw.

passage:
In the Class 6 classroom, the teacher had to leave for a meeting. "Swap and mark each other's spelling tests. Answers are on the board."
Damini marked Vandana's test and handed it back. Nine out of ten.
Vandana checked it. Her "necessary" had only one "s". Damini had missed it.
Nobody else would notice. The teacher would just copy the marks.
Vandana chewed her lip. Then she crossed out the tick, wrote eight, and walked to the teacher's desk when she came back. "It should be eight. Damini missed one."
Damini groaned. "You could've kept it!"
"I know," said Vandana.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today was SO unfair. Siddharth and two others were talking during the maths test, and Ms Iyer cancelled PE for the WHOLE class. I didn't say a word!
At lunch I told Siddharth, "It's your fault." He said, "It's her rule. I didn't cancel PE."
I kept thinking. Punishing everyone makes us angry at the talkers, not at the talking. And the quiet ones get punished for nothing.
So after lunch I asked Ms Iyer, politely, if only the talkers could miss PE. She listened. She said she'd think about it, and that maybe next time she'd give a warning first.
I'm still annoyed. But I'm glad I asked.
— Saurabh

qa.q: Who cancelled PE for the whole class?
qa.a: Ms Iyer.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling about the PE decision?
qa.a: Saurabh felt angry and wronged, because he was punished though he hadn't talked.

qa.q: What did Saurabh do that others in the class could copy?
qa.a: He thought about why the rule felt unfair and then politely raised it with the teacher.

qa.q: How does Siddharth see the punishment?
qa.a: Siddharth sees it as the teacher's rule, not his fault, and doesn't take the blame.

grounding: In his diary a child questions whether a whole-class punishment is fair and raises it politely.

passage:
On the village cricket ground, the rule was: whoever hits the ball into Maria aunty's garden is out and must fetch it.
Vishal hit a huge six that sailed into the garden. "Out!" everyone shouted.
Maria, Maria aunty's niece, who was playing too, said, "Wait. Why should a big hit be out? He hit it well."
"Because Aunty shouts."
"Then the rule should be: fetch it and say sorry, but not out."
The boys argued. Vishal said, "Only fair if it's the same for everybody."
They agreed. Vishal fetched the ball, said sorry to Maria aunty, and kept batting.

qa.q: Whose garden did the ball go into?
qa.a: Maria aunty's garden.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when everyone shouted "Out!"?

qa.q: Which part of the children's new rule made it fairer?

qa.q: How might Maria aunty see the new rule?
qa.a: Maria aunty would probably be happier getting an apology each time, instead of just angry shouting.

grounding: Village children debate whether a cricket rule's punishment is fair and change it.

passage:
At the school in Santiago, the rule was: late homework gets zero, no matter what.
Camila had been sick with fever all weekend and handed in her project on Tuesday. Zero.
Hiroshi, who sat next to her, frowned. "That's not fair. She wasn't lazy. She was sick."
"Rules are rules," said another boy.
"But the rule is to stop lazy people, not sick ones," Hiroshi said.
At the class meeting, Hiroshi and Camila suggested: late for a good reason, bring a note, no zero. The teacher listened, and the class voted. The rule changed.
Camila's project got its mark.

qa.q: What did the rule say about late homework?
qa.a: Late homework gets zero, no matter what.

qa.q: What was Hiroshi feeling when he frowned?
qa.a: Hiroshi felt it was unfair and was upset for Camila.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi and Camila do that made the change possible?

qa.q: What is it like for Camila when her project finally gets its mark?
qa.a: Camila likely feels relieved and respected, knowing her illness was taken into account.

I'm Zeenat. I still remember the day in Class 6 when I got my first period at school. I saw a stain on my skirt in the washroom and my hands went cold. I thought everyone would laugh.
I went to our class teacher. She didn't make a face. She took me to the sick room, gave me a pad and a spare skirt, and showed me how to use it. She said, "This is normal. It happens to girls as they grow."

That was it. No big deal.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 6.
Madhav came to see me today. He said his voice keeps cracking in class and two boys call him "squeaky". He'd also noticed hair growing under his arms and asked if something was wrong with him.
I told him these changes are normal, that everyone's body changes at a different time, and that he's not the only one. I gave him a simple book about growing up and suggested a daily bath and a clean vest.
He asked if I could tell the class that teasing about bodies isn't okay. I spoke to the class teacher this afternoon, and we'll do a puberty session next week. — Hafsa Qureshi

qa.q: What did the two boys call Madhav?
qa.a: "Squeaky".

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling when he asked if something was wrong with him?
qa.a: Madhav felt worried and embarrassed about his body changing and being teased.

qa.q: What did Hafsa Qureshi do that helped Madhav?
qa.a: She told him the changes are normal, gave him a book and simple hygiene tips, and acted on his request about the teasing.

qa.q: How might the boys who tease see things after the puberty session?

Dear Diary,
Today something happened. I got my period. I was at home, thank god. Amma is in Chennai for Paati's operation, so it was just Appa.
I didn't know how to tell him. I stood outside his room for ages. Finally I said, "Appa, I think I got my period."
He didn't look embarrassed. He said, "Okay. Good that you told me." He went to the medical shop and came back with pads. He'd even asked the shop lady which kind.
Then he made me hot milk and said, "If it hurts, tell me." Amma called and asked if I was okay. I said yes. I meant it.
— Kavitha

qa.a: Amma is probably relieved and grateful that Appa handled it well while she was away.

I'm Anjali, Anirban's cousin. Every evening this summer, Anirban practised his badminton serve against the wall of our building. Fifty serves. I counted once out of boredom.
At first the shuttle went everywhere. After two weeks, it hit the same brick almost every time.
Then he played the inter-colony match against a taller boy. He lost, badly. I thought he'd throw his racquet.
He didn't. He walked to the net, shook the boy's hand, and said, "Good game. Your smash is scary."
On the way home he was quiet. The next evening he was back at the wall, practising smashes.

qa.q: What might Anirban have been feeling on the quiet way home?

qa.q: How does Anjali see Anirban after the match?

Dear Diary,
Today my little brother Rinku fell off the swing and cut his knee on a stone. There was blood and he screamed.
My heart was pounding, but I remembered what we learnt in school. I took him to the tap and washed it with clean water. Then I pressed a clean hanky on it till it stopped bleeding.

passage:
It was a quiet Sunday afternoon in Malmö. Tariq was at Tomas's flat playing video games when they heard a thud from the kitchen.
Tomas's grandfather was on the floor, not answering.
Tomas froze. Tariq grabbed the phone from the table. "What's your address? Say it."
Tomas said it. Tariq dialled 112 and told the operator: "An old man fell down and isn't answering. He's breathing." He gave the address twice. The operator told them to stay with him and unlock the front door.
Tomas held his grandfather's hand. Tariq unlocked the door. The ambulance arrived in minutes.

qa.q: What number did Tariq dial?
What was Tomas feeling when he froze?
qa.a: Tomas was in shock and very scared seeing his grandfather on the floor.

qa.q: What did Tariq do that helped most?
qa.a: He called the emergency number, gave the address clearly twice, and followed the operator's instructions.

qa.q: What would change if Tariq had frozen too?
qa.a: Help would have come later, with no one giving the address or following the operator's instructions, which could have been dangerous for the grandfather.

grounding: A child in Sweden calls emergency services when a friend's grandfather collapses.

passage:
I'm Pooja. Varun sits next to me. For two weeks he's been saying he doesn't want to go to his extra swimming lesson. He picks at his nails and goes quiet when anyone says "swimming".
Today at break I asked him why. He looked around and whispered that the coach says it's their secret and touches him where his swimsuit covers. He said, "Don't tell."
I said, "This isn't a secret you should keep." I went with him straight to our class teacher.
She listened, told Varun it was not his fault, and took us both to the principal's office. The principal called Varun's parents right away and said the coach would not see any students.

qa.q: Where does Varun say the coach touches him?
qa.a: Where his swimsuit covers.

qa.q: What does Varun picking at his nails suggest?
qa.a: Varun seems anxious and upset about the swimming lessons.

qa.q: What did Pooja do that was right?
qa.a: She told Varun this is not a secret to keep and took him straight to a trusted adult that same day.

qa.q: What would change if Pooja had kept Varun's secret as he asked?
qa.a: Varun would stay alone with the problem and could keep being harmed, because no adult would know to protect him.

grounding: A classmate helps a boy report unsafe touch to a teacher, who acts the same day.

passage:
Before: In health class, the teacher taught them: "No one may touch your private parts. Say no, get away, tell a trusted adult. If the first adult doesn't help, keep telling until someone does." Lalremsiami wrote her trusted adults on a card: Mother, Bhupen, Class teacher.
During: A week later, a visiting relative asked her to play a "secret tickle game" in the bedroom and reached for her. She said, "No!" loudly and ran out. She found her big brother Bhupen and told him. Bhupen took her straight to their mother.
Their mother listened, held her and said, "You did exactly right. It's not your fault." That evening she told the relative to leave and called the child helpline.
After: The relative has not been back. Lalremsiami keeps the card in her bag.

qa.q: Who did Lalremsiami list as trusted adults?
qa.a: Mother, Bhupen and her class teacher.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when she said "No!" and ran out?
qa.a: Lalremsiami was frightened but brave, remembering what she had learned.

qa.q: What did the family do right?
qa.a: Bhupen took her straight to their mother, who believed her, said it wasn't her fault and acted that same day.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have felt when his sister told him?
qa.a: Bhupen was probably shocked and protective, and glad he could take her to their mother right away.

grounding: Over a week a child learns body safety rules and uses them, with her family acting the same day.

passage:
Sabina, you asked why I made you learn the names of your trusted adults. Let me tell you why.
When I was about your age, a man who ran the paan shop near our house used to call me in for sweets. One day he tried to touch me where my swimsuit would cover. I pushed his hand away and ran.
I was so scared I didn't want to tell. But I told my mother that same evening. She held me and said, "You did right. It's not your fault." That night she and my father went to the elders, and the shop was shut.
I was lucky: she believed me the first time. If she hadn't, I should have told someone else, and kept telling. That's what your Farida nani wants you to know.

qa.q: What did the man at the paan shop use to call Farida in for?
qa.a: Sweets.

qa.q: What was young Farida feeling when she didn't want to tell?
qa.a: Farida felt scared and perhaps ashamed, even though it wasn't her fault.

qa.q: What choice did young Farida make that evening, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She told her mother that same evening, which let an adult protect her and stop the man.

qa.q: How might Farida's mother have felt when Farida told her?
qa.a: Her mother was likely shocked and angry at the man but deeply protective of Farida, which is why she acted that night.

grounding: A grandmother tells her granddaughter how she reported unsafe touch as a child and was protected.

passage:
In the small town, Vinita kept her pocket money in a clay piggy bank. She was saving for new school shoes; her old ones had a hole.
At the Sunday fair, her sister Uma pointed at a glittery plastic tiara. "That's so pretty!"
Vinita wanted it badly. She had enough coins in her pocket.
She held the tiara. Then she thought of her wet sock last monsoon.
"Next time," she said, putting it down.
At home, she dropped her coins in the piggy bank. It was getting heavy. Uma rolled her eyes. "Boring." But Vinita smiled.

qa.q: What was Vinita saving for?
qa.a: New school shoes.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling when she held the tiara?
qa.a: Vinita felt tempted and torn between the pretty tiara and her shoes.

qa.q: What helped Vinita decide, and what could she try next time?
qa.a: Remembering her wet sock reminded her the shoes were a real need; next time she could ask a trusted adult to help her plan for both.

qa.q: How does Uma see Vinita's choice?
qa.a: Uma thinks it's boring, since she was excited about the tiara.

grounding: A child in a small town chooses her saving goal over an impulse purchase at a fair.

passage:
In Accra, Kofi was saving for football boots. His old ones pinched his toes.
After school, his friend Tomas bought a big bag of sweets and a toy car from the corner shop. "Get one too!"
Kofi looked at his coins. He loved those toy cars.
He counted in his head how many more weeks until he had enough for the boots. If he spent it now, it would be longer.
"I'll just have one of your sweets," he said.
Tomas laughed and shared. That weekend, Kofi's grandmother saw the jar and smiled. "You're nearly there."

qa.q: What was Kofi saving for?
qa.a: Football boots.

qa.q: What was Kofi feeling when he looked at his coins?
qa.a: Kofi felt tempted and torn, because he loved the toy cars but wanted the boots.

qa.q: What helped Kofi stick to his goal?
qa.a: Thinking about how spending now would delay the boots helped him choose, and a trusted adult like his grandmother can keep encouraging him.

qa.q: How might Tomas see Kofi's choice?
qa.a: Tomas doesn't seem to mind and happily shares, so it doesn't hurt their friendship.

grounding: A child in Ghana resists an impulse buy to keep saving for boots he needs.

passage:
At the school fete, each student had a small amount of pocket money to spend. Dhruv had to buy a geometry box he'd lost, and then could spend the rest.
The game stalls were loud and bright. Deepika tugged him toward the ring toss. "Win a giant teddy!"
Dhruv looked at his money, then at the stationery stall at the back.
"If I play first and lose, I won't have enough for the box."
"But the teddy!"
"The box is for exams." He bought it first. Then he played ring toss once with what was left, and missed.
He laughed anyway. "At least I've got a compass."

qa.q: What did Dhruv have to buy at the fete?
qa.a: A geometry box.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when he looked at his money and then at the stationery stall?
qa.a: Dhruv felt torn between the fun stalls and what he needed.

qa.q: What did Dhruv do that helped him handle both a need and a want?
qa.a: He bought the needed box first, then used what was left for fun.

qa.q: How might Deepika see Dhruv's choice?
qa.a: Deepika might think he's too careful at first, but she sees he still had fun after buying the box.

grounding: At a school fete, a child buys what he needs before spending on a want.
